A retrospec- tive analysis12 of the NSABP P-1 data for women who had developed invasive breast cancer found that in carriers of the oncogene BRCA2, but not BRCA1 carriers, there was a reduction in breast cancer similar to the reduction in oes- trogen-receptor positive cancer among all women in the study. The numbers available, however, were too small to be statistically significant, and it is therefore still not known if tamoxifen can reduce the risk of breast cancer in patients with these mutations. Another anti-oestrogen, raloxifene, has reportedly shown a reduction in breast cancer risk while its effects on oste- oporosis were being studied.13 A further large placebo- Antineoplastics 663 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) controlled study14 that included the incidence of breast cancer as a primary outcome also found a reduction with about 5 years of raloxifene use. There was a 55% lower risk of invasive oestrogen-receptor positive cancer (abso- lute risk reduction of 1.2 cancers per 1000 women treated for 1 year), but there was no effect on oestrogen-receptor negative disease. The effect of raloxifene has also been di- rectly compared with tamoxifen in women with a predict- ed increased risk of breast cancer.15 After up to 5 years of use, the incidence of invasive disease was similar in both groups, suggesting that raloxifene is as effective as tamoxifen in reducing the risk of developing invasive breast cancer in this group of women. The aromatase in- hibitors, anastrozole and exemestane, are also under inves- tigation.16 From these studies, tamoxifen prophylaxis has been shown to reduce the incidence of oestrogen-receptor breast cancer in women at increased risk, but there are limited data for women with BRCA1 and 2 mutations. Although the follow-up studies to date suggest that a course of tamoxifen is not merely delaying the development of breast cancer during treatment, it is not known whether this is a life-long effect; it is also not known whether over- all survival will be improved. Long-term follow-up of large placebo-controlled studies is needed to provide an- swers to these questions. Until then, it is likely there will be continued disagreement on whether tamoxifen should be used for primary prevention, and if so, in whom, and for how long. Nevertheless, the use of tamoxifen for 5 years has been recommended for women who meet specified criteria for increased risk.2,17 Raloxifene has been pro- posed by some as an alternative for women who are post- menopausal,2 but others17 do not recommend its use for breast cancer prevention.
